maintopic: NEW ORDERS IN VIEW OF SHORTAGE OF SUPPLIES
speechtext: I shall be glad to make a statement later. The position is, however, that the situation is deteriorating very rapidly. It is now over five weeks since any coal has been received from the United States into the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and it is not likely that any considerable shipments will be received for another month. Existing supplies are not sufficient to see us through, and therefore a determined effort is being made to spread out existing supplies as far as possible. maintopic: THE SUPREME COURT

speechtext: I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Justice in order that he may explain on behalf of the Supreme Court of Canada, which is denied the right of explaining, an article appearing in a recent issue of the Financial Post in regard to the Supreme Court of Canada, pointing out that, so far as the supreme court is concerned, in one case involving S200 a 37-page judgment was given by the supreme court, whereas in another case involving a man well known in public life the court refused to hear the case on the ground that less than $2,000 was in dispute. This article-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE SUPREME COURT
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "FINANCIAL POST"
speechtext:
Order. I cannot see that there is sufficient urgency in the matter which the hon. member seeks to bring to the attention of the house to justify his proceeding with the question at this time. I would suggest to him that he move for the production of papers respecting the matter.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): I am quite sure, sir, that you have not seen the article in question. If you had seen it you would have come to the conclusion, as I think most other lawyers would, that it is urgent that the misapprehension which this article might create should be cleared up, if in fact it is not true. I ask for your indulgence because I think it is a matter of genuine public interest.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE SUPREME COURT
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "FINANCIAL POST"
speechtext: I have noted the remarks of the Minister of Justice. This is not regular procedure, but to bring the matter to the attention of the house and with unanimous consent, the hon. member for Lake Centre may continue.

maintopic: THE SUPREME COURT
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "FINANCIAL POST"
speechtext:
Thank you. This article says, having regard to these cases, one of minor importance and the other in which a man formerly in public life was involved, one being hear^ and the other not:
What flashes through the minds of Canadians as they hear about this Supreme Court turndown? Could there possibly he any connection between that fact and the other fact that Mulock is influential in politics?
My question is: Will the minister explain the difference between these two cases, so that any suggestion of bias, prejudice or the suspicion of the likelihood of there being any in the supreme court, will be removed?

Mr. ST. LAURENT: The hon. member for Lake Centre is rendering a real public service in bringing this matter to the attention of the house. It came to my attention over the week-end, and I had the same misgivings about it that he had when he saw it. The title of the article is: "Our Supreme Court Should Be Careful." It then goes on to say:
Just out from the Supreme Court of Canada is a thirty-seven page judgment. Somebody is suing somebody for $200 because sixteen horses shipped from Saskatchewan arrived at Montreal with their tails cut off.
I do not know where the writer of the article got the information that there was a thirty-seven page judgment. I looked at the reports of the supreme court and that case has not yet been reported. I did not look at the Dominion Law Reports to see if it had been reported there, but I inquired about the facts, and I found that this is a case in which the supreme cpurt had no alternative but to exercise its jurisdiction.
An action for damages which involved the interpretation of the live stock bill of lading as approved by the transport commissioners had been brought, and the case was dealt with in the trial court and in the court of King's bench of the province of Quebec. After the judgment in the court of King's bench confirmed the judgment of the trial court an application for special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada was made in the court of King's bench on the ground that this was a form that was in use generally all over Canada, and that there was a matter of considerable public interest in the proper construction of that form, which was the approved form of making contracts with transportation companies for the transportation of live stock.
The Quebec court of King's bench or court of appeal, as is authorized by the Supreme Court Act, granted leave to appeal. That having been done, the supreme court had no discretion; it had to hear and dispose of the case.
In the other case, an appeal as of right was taken from the unanimous confirmation by the court of appeal of Ontario of a judgment rendered in the Ontario trial court in a case in which there was no specified amount of money involved. Under the statute and under the practice of the supreme court, confirmed by a large number of cases, that is not a case which can be appealed to the supreme court as of right. The respondent moved to quash the appeal. The supreme court heard the motion, and finding that it was not a case which could could be appealed as of right, granted the motion and declared itself without jurisdiction to hear the appeal.

Labour Conditions
It is most unfortunate that, because of the names of persons involved in the litigation, there should be any suggestion that their present or former positions in society or politics could have anything to do with the result. As a matter of fact, the house sees that the supreme court was without discretion. It so happened that when the motion for the dismissal of the appeal came before the supreme court, the chief justice was absent, and the court was presided over by Mr. Justice Patrick Kerwin, who, if there was anything in the suggestion sometimes heard that a man does not forget to which political party he belonged before he went to the bench-

maintopic: THE SUPREME COURT
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ARTICLE IN "FINANCIAL POST"
speechtext: Do not be too sure of that.

I was expecting to be asked a question about the strike of the lumber workers in British Columbia which started at two o'clock to-day. Since no hon. member has asked about it, I think the house is entitled to be informed. The facts are these. The International Woodworkers of America, through their representatives, have requested the British Columbia lumber operators for an 63260-98
increase, I understand, equal to twenty-five cents per hour and reduction of hours of work to forty per week.
Negotiations on a collective bargaining basis have been going on between the operators and a committee representing the union which resulted in an offer being made by the employers of an increase of 124 cents per hour with a reduction of the work week to forty-four hours. The union have also requested a union shop and a check-off system.
, The dispute is one which comes within provincial authority. Notification was publicized that a strike would occur to-day, and as there was evidence that the negotiations were breaking down, the Hon. George S. Pearson, Minister of Labour for British Columbia, consulted with me in the matter and recommended the appointment of a special commissioner. Accordingly I appointed Hon. Chief Justice G. McG. Sloan, of Vancouver, B.C., an industrial disputes inquiry commission-I quote from the order of appointment:
To confer with the parties and to endeavour to effect a settlement of the issues in dispute between them as aforesaid. In event that the commission is unable to bring about a settlement of the dispute, the commisison shall report to the Minister of Labour not later than thirty days after the date hereof or such longer period as may be authorized by the Minister of Labour setting out its specific recommendations as to the manner in which the dispute may be determined.
I have not had a report from Chief Justice Sloan. However, the information received by me by telephone early this morning from the British Columbia minister of labour is to the effect that at the meeting held by the chief justice yesterday the negotiations came to an end because those representing the union took the position that the strike was going to take place at eleven o'clock this morning. The operators felt that there was nothing to be gained by proceeding further with the negotiations, in view of the refusal of those representing the union to postpone the date of the strike.
Briefly the position is: (a) the union would not postpone the strike; (b) both parties were willing to arbitrate the question of union shop and union security conditionally, in so far as the operators are concerned, upon the strike being called off; (c) the union offered to settle the wage question on a basis of an increase of 18 cents per hour and a forty-hour week; (d) the operators are prepared to negotiate further on the question of wages providing the strike was called off.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in presenting the case against the increase in the prices of farm implements the other day I pointed out that according to the select special committee of the Saskatchewan legislature on farm implement prices and

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
distribution, in the year 1936 out of a cost price to the farmer of $281, some $22.62 or only eight per cent went to labour, and $71.06 or 25 per cent went into the cost of materials, so that the total cost of labour and materials came to 33 per cent, or only one-third of the total cost of a binder. I pointed out also that in the remaining costs in connection with overhead, experimental work, the cost of selling, the cost of advertising, the cost of credit, collecting bad debts and so on, the companies in the meantime had been able to effect considerable savings. So it seems to me that in a consideration of this whole question we should take the gains or savings made by the implement companies and balance them against the increased costs.
Everyone knows costs in the fields of labour and material have increased, but we have not yet considered the increased savings to the companies in these other directions. Let us take the cost of selling, for instance. Those who have lived on farms remember that it is not so long since the farmers were canvassed by the implement agents in attempts to sell them tractors or binders. It is not many years since the dealers were driving over the country roads in company with high pressure salesmen, interviewing prospects. That does not happen any more, because for several years now the office of  the small town agent has been haunted by farmers clamouring for the privilege of buying implements for cash, and it is now a matter of being put on the list and trying to get a preferred position. No longer do the companies need to spend money trying to sell farm implements. The farmers are begging to buy. No longer do the companies need to indulge in high priced advertising, because the farmer is not fussy any more. He does not insist on a Massey-Harris tractor or an Allis-Chalmers tractor; he takes any tractor or combine he can get. So there must be considerable savings in the fields of advertising and salesmanship. Also in the fields of financing and the collection of bad debts these costs must have been wiped out. Not only does the farmer pay cash, but even in previous years the companies took care of that situation by increasing the cash price to the buyer and making the man who paid cash carry the risk of the man who bought on credit. I submit therefore that in these fields the company has effected considerable saving.
What about the pre-war picture? The prewar picture seems now to be accepted, just as we accepted excess profits as being excess in relation to normal profits. We seem to have accepted the pre-1939 structure of farm implement prices as legitimate. Time and usage have sanctified the position of the companies. But the report of the special select 63260-98J
committee on farm implement prices did not. It condemned very strenuously the practices of the company, and recommended that certain steps be taken to remove these abuses of power in a field where the producer of farm implements had the whip hand over the consumer, the man who bought them.
These abuses have not been remedied. Although tariffs were reduced to allow more competition in the field, every time the tariff came down, the price paid by the farmer and the profits collected by the company went up. That is why no one should accept this new price increase without question. Increases are based on established abuses, not upon a just price structure.
This is a strong indictment of the attitude and policy of implement manufacturers. Their whole practice is built, not oh cooperation with the workers in the industry and the farmers whom they serve, but upon how much profit they can secure and how far they can go in defying governments. Yet this government took evidence and advice from no other body when the increase in the price of farm implements was being considered. When permission was given for an advance in prices, the manufacturers were the only people consulted. This is a breach in the wall of price control, a wall which the Progressive Conservative party wishes to demolish even more rapidly by removing all price controls. This is another victory for big business, and its control over the family income and over the homes of thousands of Canadian men, women and children.
We in this group have consistently supported the government in its price control policy as applied to the things the farmer has to buy, and its policy of stabilized prices for the things he has to sell. In other words, we have supported a proper price relationship.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis):
That all the words following the word "government's" in the amendment, in the last paragraph of page 184 of Votes and Proceedings, llay 6, 1946, to the word "imposing" in the second line of the amendment, be struck out and the following words be substituted therefor:
"policies permitting recent unjustifiable increases in the prices of farm machinery and of steel hare resulted in" and that the amendment be further amended by inserting the words:
"and workers" after the word "producers" in the third line of the amendment, so that it would then read:
"This house is of the opinion that the government's policies of permitting recent unjustifiable increases in the prices of farm machinery and of steel have resulted in imposing on food producers and workers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies."

It seems clear therefore that the farmer in Canada has benefited by a better control of this element in his costs, and I should add that there is reason to believe that further increases will be announced very shortly in the United - States for particular companies.
I have not taken very much of the time of this house on any occasion during the last two or three years, and particularly in the last two sessions. But I should like now to have the privilege which some have, as a back-bencher not attached to any department of government, and to present some of my own reactions and make some statements which I have wanted to make as a result of things which have been said in this house.
It might be inferred from something which I have said that I am making a point for the farm implement companies. I am doing nothing of the kind, and I am satisfied that the wartime prices and trade board was not doing so either. The board wanted to see a steady and increasing flow of farm machinery to the farmers, particularly at this time when we are in short supply, and that was the main motive of their adjustment. I feel certain that, had I been sitting in the place of the members of that board, looking at the matter from the point of view of Canada as a whole, I would have adopted very much the same position. However, were I to turn myself around and put myself in the seat of the managers of some of these larger manufacturing concerns, I am not just sure what my reaction would have been. I rather think that I would have hesitated; I would have waited for a clearer sign of what my production possibilities were going to be before I made my application. However, they have made that application; and I think that the board, in the light of their financial standing, in the light of the costs of their equipment, and in the light of the need for farm machinery, did the right thing.
Generally speaking, this might indicate that I am not a believer in high prices, but I assure you that I am a believer in high prices. I believe in high prices as long as those prices can be controlled. High prices, high wages and high standards of living go hand in hand. But I am opposed to anything which would mean, for this country, inflation. In my opinion inflation and sudden decontrols would be very detrimental, and I will oppose them with all the vigour that I can command.	.
I have in my hand a chart-I do not know whether many hon. members can see it or not

-indicative of where prices ran to in 1919, shortly after the war. Prices ran as high as 300 per cent above normal. Those who are close enough to see this chart will notice that it represents a bare triangle; there is a sharp rise and a very sudden fall in prices. What the wartime prices and trade board are trying to do is to prevent this rapid increase and this rapid fall. If the Canadian people will give the board support in maintaining a reasonable level of prices-not a permanent rigid structure without adjustments here and there as they become necessary, but the holding of the line on a reasonable level, cutting off this absurd peak at the top-the people will be spared untold hardship and discouragement.

If you take the controls off, prices will be higher. I do not think any hon. member can accuse me of once having interrupted him when he was speaking, and I would ask that the same courtesy be shown to me that I have extended to everyone else.
The inference has been left in this house by some hon. members that business men, particularly manufacturers, are anxious to see large pools of unemployed men in this country so that at a moment's notice they can reach out and bring in whatever men are necessary to meet seasonal demands, and thereby get cheap labour, and as soon as the temporary demand is satisfied, let them go back again on relief. I assure you that such a view is entirely opposite to good business, and is the very reverse of the view held by the men with whom I associate most. A man who is unemployed, who is walking the streets without any money in his pocket, without a pay envelope coming in weekly, is not a customer of anybody. The one thing that a business man wants, be he a retailer or a merchant of any kind, is customers, and in order to obtain customers, people must be working. So far as I know the feelings of the group of people whom I represent, it is their firm desire that the men and women of this country shall be fully employed.
A further view, and in my opinion an eiToneous one, held in some places is that manufacturers want the farmers to be in receipt of low prices. They do not want to see anything of the kind. The view I have here expressed more often than anything else

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
is that we want to see the first four large producers of primary products in Canada operating at capacity and at reasonably good prices. The first of these groups is the farmer. We want to see every farmer at work, extra men employed on his farm turning out the maximum of production, and we want to see him receiving the maximum return for his product. There again, if you like, the selfish motive comes into play, and there is where we shall find an outlet for our secondary goods.
Secondly, we want to see the lumber companies and those working in the woods operating, not to the capacity of the saw mills to cut lumber but to the capacity of the nation to regrow the forests that are cut year by year; otherwise the product would run out. However w'e want to see that industry running as fully as it can.
We want to see the mines, the third primary industry, in full production; and in addition we want to see the fourth primary producer, a very important one so far as British Columbia is concerned, operating to capacity. I refer to the fishermen and those dealing in fish products.
We maintain that by giving these people full employment, putting them all in a position where they can be actively engaged, those who are engaged in secondary'industries will not have difficulty in keeping the rest of the men and women in Canada fully employed. That chiefly is the position I take. If you like to regard it as selfish, you can do so, but it is good business, and the two go together. Let me say this, however, that in my opinion while selfishness will succeed for a time, eventually the man who employs only selfish tactics in his own business will lose out, because selfishness is bound to ruin anyone who uses it to further his own needs only.
Our fight in this house therefore-and it is one that should receive the support of every group here-is to see that the man who desires an undue profit on his own goods, thus creating a spiral, shall not be allowed to have his way. I think we have every right to ask for the. full support of the house for any move in that direction.
I know that adjustments have to be made from time to time; I am prepared to support any necessary adjustments. Adjustments, however, must be timed, and they must be orderly if they are not to ruin the country. What I am particularly concerned about is not the cost of the end products, but the cost of the basic products; and I consider that any wide jump in the price of wheat, which is not an end product in itself-I think it may be
regarded as the cornerstone, so to speak, of many other products in the country-would not be to the advantage of the farmers themselves or to the advantage of the people of Canada as a whole.

speechtext:
I know that the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Mayhew) is sincere in his presentation to the house and believes everything he says. I have a high regard for him. I believe however that in his attempt this afternoon to justify the increased price of farm machinery there are one or two things he overlooked. Personally I am not very much impressed by figures prepared by those who were responsible for granting the increase. They may or may not be correct; we have no way of checking them.
There are one or two things which I would ask the hon. gentleman to explain with regard to the hand-out of 12i per cent given the farm implement companies. I would like him to check up on how much of that was due to changing their capital structure. The member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) a few evenings ago put on the record the fact that they had given their higher employees gifts of blocks of stock that ran into a considerable amount of money. That is something that should be checked.
Second, I would ask the hon. member to check and some time inform the house how much they are losing in their export trade. Are they losing in exporting at the present time in order to establish their export markets, taking it out of the home market?
Third, one statement which the hon. member made jarred me a bit. He said that an increased price was granted these companies because of the fact that they were in short supply. In effect, the government was desirous of seeing maximum production in the field of agriculture, but they could not get it because there was a shortage of farm implements. The farm implement companies were in a position to sit back and say, "We will export; we do not have to sell here. If you get implements you will get them on our terms". That was the impression that I got, and that in effect is to sabotage an important industry and is an indictment against any organization that takes that attitude because of a shortage or because of the crisis that exists. These are a few of the things I would like to have clarified.
In rising to take part in this debate there are a few things on which I feel strongly. First I was disappointed, when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) moved his amendment, that he confined the discussion exclusively to agriculture. In my opinion
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

there is no possible solution in looking at the problem as it pertains to one section of society. Unless the whole economy of the country is healthy, there is no possibility of improving the situation for any one particular section of that economy.
My impression of the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition was that it was the thin end of the wedge to get away from price controls, taking advantage of a problem in the country to-day in regard to which there is a good deal of agitation, quarrelling with the government's position in the matter of price controls, and starting t-o chisel in that direction. I was disappointed that the hon. gentleman did not include the whole economy of the country so that we might have it thoroughly discussed. However, the subamendment moved by the member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) now opens up that discussion.
I do not think anyone in the house is doubtful as to where the Progressive Conservative party stands in regard to price controls, and I agree with the statement made by the member for Victoria in this regard. This group believes in realistically handling that situation and in having a real price control, but I am afraid that the government, while making statements in the house and in the press, and the wartime prices and trade board, while expressing anxiety to maintain price controls and protect the consumer, are only rendering lip service, and that secretly they are doing the same thing that the Conservative party stands for only they are not doing it in the open.
Price controls are being removed, and removed rapidly. They started with the farm implement companies and the basic steel industries; they granted increases in the products from the top, which is bound to be reflected in the cost to the consumer. Once that kind of thing is started there is no getting away from it.
Let' us take the list of some four hundred articles and commodities in Canada in respect of which price controls have been removed. If one examines the lists sent out by the wartime prices and trade board he will find that there is not very much price control on the things that the average person has to buy in Canada to-day. Go down town and buy a hat; you will pay $1.50 more for it than you would have paid two weeks ago. Buy a shit of clothes and you will have to do exactly the same thing. It is true all along the line. Controls are being removed from the very things that the average person has to buy.
I suggest that any hon. member on the govern-
ment benches who means what he says with regard to price controls should carefully check and find out what is going on.
We got into this spiral when we made the first bow to the steel companies. An increase was granted to the basic steel industry which automatically reflected itself in the price of implements made by the farm implement companies. They came along and asked for an increase. They will all come along and ask for the same consideration. If the controls are dropped from all the basic commodities of Canada, we shall not have price control very long.
This afternoon I should like to go into the other side of the story. The farmers' side of the picture has been handled capably. I am in agreement with the statement made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar with regard to stabilization of farm commodities, parity prices and so forth, and there is no need for me to repeat it.
The government made its first mistake when it granted the increase to the basic steel industries of Canada without any consultation with the general public or with the employees of the steel companies. The increase was granted despite the fact that the steelworkers' union of Canada have been patient and long-suffering, particularly in the community from which I come. They have been trying to get an adjustment in their wage rates for thd last four years, in order to wipe out the differential which exists between themselves and the rest of the industry in Canada.

When the steel manufacturers of Canada were granted an increase of $5 in the price of basic steel they were called in

and the matter was discussed with them. It was also given to the manufacturers in Sydney, despite the fact that they are subsidized. According to the statement I saw in the press, a certain portion of that increase was supposed to be used for the purpose of increasing wages; but when the steelworkers' union approached the wartime prices and trade board and asked what portion of that increase was to go to paying wages, they were told to go out and see the steel companies and iron it out with them. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) knows that until a week ago the union has not been able to meet the steel companies; the companies would not meet them. In effect the wartime prices and trade board said this: Go out and fight it out with the companies yourselves. They have got the $5 increase on basic steel; a share of that is yours; go and get it. That kind of attitude promotes industrial strife. They should have been consulted. The proportion of that increase which was allocated for the purpose of increasing wages should have been determined, and the steelworkers' union should have been informed about it. That was not done.
Since this session opened hon. members have been lobbied by the steelworkers' union, by the packing-house workers, by coal miners, electrical workers, and shipyard workers. I am of the opinion that this country is on the verge of an industrial upheaval. The Minister of Labour realizes that. It should be headed off. The demands of the workers are not so great. The steelworkers' union is a good case in point. If there is any organization in this country which has been patient and long-suffering, which has canvassed every legal piece of machinery available in an effort to iron out its difficulties, it is the steelworkers' union. It is a national organization. In the lobby they put on in the house the majority of the members signed a statement which said that their case was just, that their demands were reasonable and that they would back them in getting their demands. What were their demands? They were conservative. They asked for a minimum weekly wage of $36, a forty-hour week, two weeks' vacation with pay, tax exemptions up to $2,000, and a tri-partite council consisting of the employers, the employees and members of the government to sit together to iron out their difficulties and come to an understanding, instead of doing what they are doing now, declaring war on each other. These are their demands. They are conservative when considered in the light of the wage rates in the same industry in the L'nited States.
So long as there exists a differential between the standards of living in the different sections of society in Canada and the United States, we are going to have difficulties in this country. It is bound to flow over here. The workers of Canada know what the wages are in the United States; they know what the standards are. A lot of our unrest to-day is based on the fact that our standards are so low in comparison with similar occupations in the United States. These unions are international unions; they are part and parcel of the United States set-up. They hold joint conventions; they exchange literature. The average worker in this country knows just how far his standards are below the standards in the United States. In most industries I think there is a differential of about 30 per cent as between Canada and the United States, and something must be done to level that off. There is also a difference in the cost of living; I realize that, but it is not equal to the differential in the income of the workers. I do not care how high the cost of living goes; if you have wage rates which are comparable and which enable you to buy. I do not believe shrinking the pay envelope or the income of the people of this country is going to solve our problem. On the contrary it is going to get us back to where we were in 1939. One of the first things President Truman did in the United States on the cessation of hostilities was to instruct industry in that country that wage rates must be brought up by something like 25 to 30 per cent, so that the

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: That increase in the United States has gone down the drain already because of inflation.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: I would not say that. There is a whole lot of the bogey man in this business of inflation. I am not very much afraid of it. We talk about the difference between the cost of living to-day and the cost of living in 1919 and 1920, but some time I should like the Minister of Finance to put alongside those figures the rates of taxation in the two periods, so that the public may see how much worse off they are to-day. You are getting it in a different way this time. After the last war it was put on a pair of shoes, a pair of socks, a can of milk and so on, where everybody could see it. To-day it is being taken away from the worker by a very heavy income tax and then passed back to the industrialists and manufacturers under the table by way of subsidies, so it is hidden. The profits made during this war by the industrialists and manufacturers of this country were higher than those made during the last war; make no mistake about that. This business of waving that flag of inflation is overdone. A little inflation is good, if it does not get away from you. If you mean your price controls, when you get the thing where you want it and control it for ever I do not think you will have any difficulty. But I do not believe you are controlling anything to-day; that is my opinion. You go out to buy anything in this country and you will find that the price has taken quite a jump since the end of the war. I have a few figures here. I believe the cost of living index in this country is crazy. I do not believe anyone who compiled that cost of living index can justify it by any reasonable means to any sensible person. I do not think it reflects the cost of living in this country at all. I would ask any hon. member of this house to have a committee in his community go out and check the merchants, the fellows who are retailing. Take their inventories in 1939 and their inventories to-day; compare them with the cost of living index as put out by the government, and you will find a great discrepancy.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: And check the quality of the material.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS

We have sent out committees of the mineworkers union to canvass Sydney, Glace Bay, New Waterford and so on, and we can show you figures gathered from the merchants, showing their inventories and the prices at which they were selling at a certain date, and so on. According to these figures the cost of living in that section of the community in 1942 was up around thirty per cent in the essentials the average person had to buy. Do not forget that about eighty or eighty-five per cent of the cash handled by the average small salaried man or wage earner in this country is spent on food, clothing and shelter, particularly on food. That does not include any luxuries. When you put the increase on a pound of butter and a pound of bacon, and on clothing, you are hitting him one hundred per cent. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Be a little bit fair, will you not?

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I am trying to be. The fact of the matter is that I am bending over backwards to try to make it easy for the Minister of Finance, because I appreciate his difficulties.
On the other side of the picture, in reference to this business of profits, I refer to a recent survey by the Bank of Canada-and Graham Towers does not make any mistakes. This comes from his organization. The net profits of Canadian business institutions in 1944 were double those of 1936. Accumulated surpluses and reserves by 700 companies in 1943 amounted to $1,188 million as compared to $800 million in 1938. Wages have not gone up proportionately.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: The hon. member does not say that the profits after taxation were double those of 1936, does he?

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: That is right; after taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: I will have to check that.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
You check it, and you will find it is worse than I am saying. I am really making it easy for the minister. According to recent statistics given out by the dominion bureau of statistics, 611 Canadian plants with

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
a total of 108,308 hourly employees-this is where your wages are going-as of December 1, 1945, the average employee received 67 cents per hour, which compares with a rate of 70-5 cents as of December 1, 1944. In other words they suffered a reduction of over 3 cents per hour in that period of time. Three cents an hour has been actually chiselled off.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The hon. member takes
business and makes a comparison between 1936 and the present time.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Between 1936 and 1943.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Well, what about taking the same period for wages, and making a comparison between those years?

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I think it would be a good idea, but I have not the figures here just now. That is the job of the Minister of National Revenue. He should know more about wages than anybody else in this country, because he is getting most of them by way of taxation.
The point I was going to make is this. As I said a moment ago, President Truman ordered an upward trend in wages in order that the people might have purchasing power, because if they cannot buy we are going to have unemployment. The trend in Canada is the reverse. According to the dominion bureau of statistics, hourly rates of wages in Canada have dropped by approximately 3 cents. But in addition, has anybody checked how much purchasing power the Canadian dollar lost in the last year through price increases? I would not say this figure is accurate, but I did hear that in . essential commodities the Canadian dollar has lost about 16 per cent of the purchasing power it had a year ago. In other words it costs you that much more to buy things. A $4 hat has gone up by $1.50; I bought one myself only a few days ago, and I know. The cost of a suit of clothes has gone up, and so on; and mind you, you are not getting the article you got in 1939, by a long shot. The values are away down as far as material is concerned. As I said before, the trend in Canada is back to 1939. There is no doubt in my mind about that. That is the attitude of big business in this country to-day.
A few minutes ago the hon.'member for Victoria, B.C., spoke about secondary industries, and with much of what he said I can agree. I believe that not many of the secondary industries, these small decentralized industries which are standing on their own feet, are being heavily subsidized. Those fellows are square, if they have an opportunity. But there are a few large monopolies across the country which are squeezing the small fellows 63260-991	'	[DOT]
out of the picture. If the present trend continues for another four or five years there will be no secondary industry left. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is from Nova Scotia. All he has to do is to look back in that province for the past ten or fifteen years and he will see that about fifteen fairly substantial secondary industrial set-ups have been siphoned off and swallowed up by monopoly control. In fact, as recently as the period of the war, one industry, which had existed for over thirty years, expired. A few people who are connected with monopolistic industry are to-day running the show. Unfortunately the government is subsidizing them, carrying them along and keeping them in the picture.
I should like to focus the minister's attention upon the difference between the condition of the average person and that of the industrialist. Certain statutory regulations were put out on February 18, 1946. The first of these was order in council P.C. 254, dealing with the rehabilitation allowance to veterans. I shall not read it in detail, because it is lengthy. May I state briefly that it makes provision for some relief when a veteran is out of employment awaiting a course. This is restrictive and narrow, and comes back to the old system of relief. But the veteran who is not about to take any course, who may not wish to take one, or who may not be qualified to do so receives nothing. There are about 30,000 unemployed in the maritime provinces to-day. Of that number about 4,100 are on the island of Cape Breton; and of this group about 1,600 are war veterans. Most of them cannot take vocational training courses because they have not the necessary educational qualifications. Under the regulation one must have reached at least the eighth grade, and if that grade has not been reached, he does not qualify. Many of those men did not reach that grade because they did not have the clothes in which to go to school during the years of depression. They get nothing.
I turn to another order in council, P.C. 358, which makes provision for underwriting the losses, or guaranteeing the profits-one may interpret it in either way-of the Dominion Shipping company, a subsidiary of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation. This company conveys the ore from Newfoundland to the Sydney steel plant, a distance of only about ninety miles. The government has found it necessary to pass a special order in council underwriting the losses of that subsidiary of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation.
On the one hand is the boy who has just come back from overseas after fighting a
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

war. In this house for five years we were saying that nothing would be too good for him. He could have a new world, a' new heaven and a new earth. He is the fellow who saved us from ourselves. Well, he is back, and he is back on relief. There is no subsistence allowance for that man who cannot qualify for a course; and there is a limit of twelve months even for the one who is qualified. On the other hand those who stayed at home, the boards of directors, the bondholders in companies such as the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation are protected by orders in council, so that they may be guaranteed that every dollar they invest will produce a certain income. Those people are comfortable; they have good homes. They have everything they want. They have bank accounts. They are not suffering; they are not in need. But the dollar they invest is guaranteed a return by the Dominion of Canada. On the other hand, the fellow who fought the war and who saved us from the stupidity of people who have been running this world for the past thirty or forty years, comes back here and finds he is not even entitled to eat. He has no home, because the insurance companies cannot make money out of him under the national housing scheme.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Correct.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: And in many cases they have run out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: And unemployment insurance has run out. They have no jobs and no prospects of jobs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: The subsidies about which the hon. member has been speaking are to keep industry going so that they can give jobs. That is the only reason for them.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
But there has been no expansion in those industries. They are not going any farther. They are not hiring any of the boys who are coming back. There has been no expansion in those industries, and there are no jobs for them when they come back. And not only the ones who have come back, but hundreds who left school since the beginning of the war are now looking for employment.

When I asked the Minister of Labour a
few days ago, as a result of several telegrams, whether the government would consider the possibility of extending out-of-work benefits to soldiers until they could find some employment, or continuing unemployment insurance until those receiving it might be in a position to secure employment, his answer was discouraging. In effect, his answer was no, that the matter had not been considered, and that relief in any community was the responsibility of provincial and municipal governments. That is the philosophy of the thirties. It is not good enough to-day. I appreciate the necessity for subsidies under present conditions. If they are taken from any of the industries in Nova Scotia which are receiving them, those industries will fold up. But surely this is some indication that there must be a reexamination of the whole economic set-up.	^
The farmer asks for increased prices. Fine; I agree with that. I believe those prices have to be stepped up. But when we increase the price of farm products we automatically increase the cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: True.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: And that comes back to the industrial worker. If farm prices are going up, then in proportion to those increases in farm prices we have to increase the wage structure if we are to keep on an even keel. Unless this is done, the effect will be that of dumping an additional load on the shoulders of the small salaried worker. He is not in a position to pay for any increased cost of living, owing to the taxes he is paying. Certainly those who were on fixed incomes during the war took it on the chin; but I do not think the business man did, at least not to any great extent. I am amazed when I read, in the income tax form, the exemptions the business man can claim for income tax purposes. But the civil servant receiving $2,500 a year, or the wage earner receiving $25 or $30 a week, can write in nothing by way of expenses. His total income is taxed, and taxed heavily. The man who is operating a business has his expenses deducted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS

However, the attitude taken by the industrialists of this country, which apparently has been confirmed by the Department of Labour, is-

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS

him that the price of basic steel was increased S5 per ton and you told the workers to go out and fight it out with the employers.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: You are talking to the Minister of Labour now.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: The job of the Minister of Labour is to work for the good of labour. If Donald Gordon is making the minister's job any tougher than it should be, the minister should tell this house about it; the minister should get tough with him. That sort of thing promotes industrial strife in this country. I do not want to see these steelworkers in a fight, because there are too many of them in my riding. The packinghouse workers should not be permitted to get into difficulties, . because food is the main requirement of the world to-day. We should be producing the maximum of everything we can, and there should be understanding in that industry right along the line. I think that can be done.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Only three months ago I set up a commission to settle the packinghouse dispute.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I am not so sold on commissions. They just write reports. We are facing an emergency to-day similar to the one we faced during the war. The only difference is that the firing has ceased. The situation to-day is just as tense; the war has simply shifted to the home front. We should not permit these things to happen, because they are not necessary.
The Department of Labour set up a building industry council, made up of employers, employees and representatives of the government. When a dispute arises in that industry you do not hear anything about it. They get together, they arrive at an understanding, and the men go back to work. Why cannot the same sort of set-up be provided in all these industries that are facing disputes at the present time? The steelworkers' union has been asking for this for the last two years. There should be set up a tripartite council so that these problems can be talked over, so that the different parties may meet one another. If the industry does not want to do it, then the minister should set up such a council and ask them to take part.
There should not be any interruption in the production of steel. The position here is similar to that pertaining in connection with fuel. When your fuel supply is tied up, your whole economy is tied up; if the fuel supply is cut off, your plants and factories must shut
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

down. If you cut off the supply of basic steel, your fabricating plants will be tied up, as well as many other industries across the country. As far as I can see, the production of steel is going to be tied up. They have taken a strike vote which has been practically unanimous from one end of the industry to the other. If some reasonable settlement is not arrived at, this production will stop.
The labour relations board, that is the O'Connor board, is getting into difficulty. I do not intend to make any accusations, but I have received a number of letters protesting against certain actions of this board-or rather of the chairman of the board, who does not seem to be acting as an impartial chairman should. In connection with McCormick's Limited application he has been accused of casting the deciding vote to permit the establishment of a company union. If that is so, it should not have been done. I notice from press clippings that the mine workers of Nova Scotia, the steelworkers, the mine, mill and smelter workers are protesting against that action in that particular case. The application for the establishment of a company union was rejected twice by the labour relations board of Ontario because financial assistance was being provided by the company. This is the sort of thing that creates strife, because it builds up a lack of confidence in the board. The chairman is supposed to be impartial. I understand that in this particular case the labour representatives on the board dissented.
It is a rambling statement I have been making, but I mention these things because I feel that they must be taken care of if we are going to get through this period.
I should like to say something to the Minister of Finance about this matter of price controls. I believe he is in earnest and wants to do a good job in that field, but I tell him not to be fooled by some of his officials who may be kidding him that there is really price control in this country. Actually there is a lot of chiselling going on. We know just where this party stands. They want to take them off and go out and carry on under the old tooth and claw law.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Do not say "this . party," say "Conservative."

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The Conservative party. They want to climb on their neighbours' backs and get all they can for themselves. They want the old rugged individualism-to the swift the

race. If you are strong enough, trim the other fellow. Get something for yourself. That is their philosophy. They may varnish and polish it up by saying that they are getting so much money for agriculture or labour; they may say what they like about it, but I am awfully glad they are not sitting over there. All they can do here is talk about it, and I think everybody is getting wise to them.
I tell the minister not to be fooled by people who may be just giving him lip service. He may have a lot of Tories on his administrative staffs, but the fact is there is a lot of chiselling going on. I agree with the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., who says, "Hold the .line." However, I do not want just to hold the line and then keep the clamps on about eighty per cent of our people who are at the bottom. We should also hold the line at the top. If you start jacking up the prices for the manufacturers, then you increase manufacturing costs, which in turn increases the cost to the consumer. The whole thing will get into a spiral, and you will never get out of it. You have to hold it at both ends. We will back you in any control that is necessary.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS

I would not bring iup all these points if I did not have a constructive suggestion to make to him, and it is just this. We have parliamentary' committees of this house. If any hon. member has reason to doubt the ability of officials who prepare such figures or the correctness of official figures which are issued we have an instrument at our disposal; we can check their correctness; and I say to my hon. friend, in all good friendship, that if he doubts the correctness of the cost of living index he should take the matter up with the bureau-
Mr./GILLIS: I have done that many times.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
-get the information, as I have done, as to how they prepare it. Then, if he is not satisfied, he should bring the matter before a parliamentary committee where he will get a proper hearing. Obviously we cannot adequately go into a matter of this kind on the floor of the house. But let him follow the matter to a satisfactory conclusion.
The same thing applies in regard to these implement companies. In principle, the C.C.F. party is apparently in complete agreement with the government in so far as price controls are concerned, but we are as far apart as the two poles in our opinion as to the need for the increase in the selling prices of agricultural implements. We have machinery whereby those figures can be checked and verified. I am told-maybe I am wrong and my hon. friends across the floor are right-that for the past number of years the agricultural implement industry have been producing implements at an actual loss, but they have been making sufficient profits on their war contracts to offset that loss, to considerably more than offset it. The time has, however now arrived when these war contracts are no longer in existence and when the implement industry must stand on its own feeet. If what I am
told is correct, my hon. friends across the house should support the wartime prices and trade board in approving that increase. If my information is incorrect I, too, should be opposing the increase. Let us go at this matter in a businesslike way, find out who is right, check the figures, and then act accordingly.
I seldom take the time of the house to express my views on anything but an important subject. But as I pondered in my office the motion of want of confidence which was made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) on May 6, ai^d as I have listened to the speeches which were made on that motion, I felt that I would be remiss in my duty if I did not express my views. I feel strongly that the time has arrived when we should make up our minds as to which way we are going. The time has arrived when we should decide whether we want inflation as we experienced it after the last war or whether we do not want it. I do not think anyone who went through the distressing times which we had during that last inflationary period wants a recurrence of it; and I was surprised that the hon. member for Cape Breton South brushed off so blithely the "bogey of inflation", as he termed it. I was wondering where he was when we went through those distressing times after the last war, and privately I am going to ask him some time. I went through those times, and I do not want a recurrence. Every hon. member knows who suffers during an inflationary period, which is always followed by a deflationary period.

speechtext:
That
is why we did not want to see the price ceilings broken.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I am happy that my hon. friend says that; I have been happy to hear him repeat it so often in the house, and I think we can get together, because we are not so far apart in our viewpoints.
As I say the time has arrived when we must make a decision as to which way we are going. We know the government's policy. We have many times had an expression from the leader of the C.C.F. party and members of that party; they have announced their policy. As far as the government policy is concerned, it is, as I understand it, simply this, that we shall retain the price ceiling and the various controls which were so necessary and worked so satisfactorily during the war, just so long only as we must retain them in order to keep our economy on an even keel, and that we shall get rid of those controls just as quickly as that can be done with safety.
As far as the C.C.F. party is concerned, I do not want them to take offence at what I

Price Ceiling-Farm Products '
am now going to say, but I am saying it because I believe it to be true. They agree with us in principle, but time after time I have noticed that when some group, representing labour or the farmers or some other interest, comes here wanting an improvement in its individual position, the C.C.F. party, instead of sticking to its established principle, is willing to bend it at that place even though it should throw the whole price structure out of control.	<

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: That is wrong.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: If I am wrong I am happy to "find I am wrong, and I hope that when the vote comes on the motion of the Conservative party, as it will in a few days the C.C.F. party will vote to prove I am wrong.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: I hope the hon. member will vote for our sub-amendment.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
As to the Conservatives, I think the time has arrived when the leader and the party itself, in fairness to themselves and to the country, should announce what their policy is in regard to price control. The country is entitled to know that. Down to date I have not heard any official declaration as to where the party stands with regard to the price ceiling and these controls. So far the party has contented itself with flank attacks on price controls. No one other than, perhaps, the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) has had courage enough to rise in his place and say positively that he wants all the controls removed at once. The party up to date has contented itself with flank attacks. This particular motion is another flank attack, and in introducing the motion the leader of the party was very careful to omit, or at any rate he did omit, to say anything at all about his party's policy in regard to controls.
As to the general policy of the government, let us take labour first. I have heard many people say that labour throughout the war has profited more than any other group. But when I look at the Labour Gazette for March, 1946, at page 335, I find in a table there showing the number of employees as reported on January 1, 1946, in the different groups covered by that table, that approximately 1,717,000 employees receive an average weekly wage of $29.85. I ask the house this question: Under present-day living conditions and costs, can any married man rear a family on a smaller amount per week? I say no. So that to those who argue in that way, and if the Conservative opposition feels that the ground for the present motion is that labour is getting too much, I suggest that these figures adequately answer that contention.

I concede at once that in certain isolated instances it is possible that considerations were extended to some small groups of labour which were too generous; but in discussing the whole problem of the price structure and controls, we cannot get anywhere by simply referring to isolated cases. I submit that we must look at the broad picture of the total figures, taking averages rather than individual instances.
To come to the farm group, what has happened there? I have a statement from the bureau of statistics showing that the farm income in 1939 was $722-3 million; that is the cash farm income. I concede at once that the industry was a depressed industry at that time, but may I point out to the leader of the opposition that, while agricultural income was $722-3 million in 1939 and the industry was then in a distressed condition, the distress at that time was nothing like what it was in the early thirties when the party of his adoption was in power. Following down from 1939, I find that in 1945 the cash farm income had more than doubled over 1939. It is now $1,654 million.
When the leader of the opposition launches this motion and makes the bald statement that agriculture is not being properly treated in the present price structure, I ask him to be good enough to indicate by what percentage farm income should be increased to bring it up to parity or an amount commensurate with the receipts of labour, of the manufacturer, and of the other groups in the country. Obviously 3rou cannot advance one without considering all the others, and if the leader of the opposition honestly thinks agriculture is not to-day receiving its fair share of the national income, the least he could do would be to indicate to the house the percentage by which he considers it is being unfairly treated.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: I say this to the hon. member for Haldimand. and I thank him for the question. I think that, compared -with the total national income and with the taxes of all the groups in Canada to-day, agriculture is getting a proper proportionate share of the total as far as it is possible for any human being to bring this about. A man would need to be a Solomon to do any better.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
This motion is a want of confidence motion because, if it carries, the government resigns. Surely that type of motion is not to be made on any irresponsible or ill-considered grounds, and the least the leader of the opposition can do is to indicate to the house the percentage by which he thinks agriculture is being unfairly treated: Then, having done that, he must not stop there. His duty does not end there. He should then frankly admit, "It is true that if we increase agriculture, say, ten per cent, giving it another S160 million, the cost of living goes up". Then he should frankly tell the house, "In view of that increase in the cost of living, I think labour should receive an additional percentage", and he should indicate what in his opinion should be that percentage. After he gets through with that, with wages having increased, and manufacturers' costs having undoubtedly increased, he should indicate to the house to what extent he thinks the manufacturer should be permitted to increase the wholesale selling price of his products.
If anyone is dissatisfied with our present price structure, is that not the obvious thing for him to do, to explain the reasons for his dissatisfaction, keeping in mind all the different groups; because, after all, no one likes price control; no one likes wage control. These controls were imposed as a matter of necessity; the necessity continues, and until it passes we must have them. It is, therefore, only natural that all the different groups should . selfishly take their own viewpoint.
But that is no reason why a responsible member of the house should not advance some sound reasons before moving a want of confidence motion asking that the government resign office because of the unfair way it is treating a certain group. I have yet to hear one word of proof from the leader of the opposition in justification of that motion.
I come now to the actual motion itself. I am now coming to my quarrel with the leader of the opposition, if you wish to put it in that way, and I am glad that he is here, because I want to talk to him. Speaking to the house on May 6, he stated, as reported at page 1244 of Hansard:
I wish, therefore, to raise a question of major< importance to the chief primary industry of this country and to the country itself, namely-
And this is the matter he wanted to raise. -the inequitable position in which agriculture now finds itself and the lessened production as a result of that inequity.
I should like to read two or three other quotations to make it clear beyond all shadow of doubt what was said on that day, because I think my hon. friend will be a little bit ashamed and apologetic of the stand he took at that time. He went on to say that production in agriculture is lower now than it was last year. Then at page 1245 of Hansard he said this:
On the whole, farm production in Canada has been declining since 1944; 1945 was lower than 1944, and 1946 will be lower than 1945. I suggest that, if the farmers were given the necessary stimulus to produce, the situation would be greatly improved.
I suggest that if these words mean anything at all they mean that the farmer has lessened the production of food in this country because the prices are not satisfactory to him. Knowing the farmers of my riding as well as I do, and admiring as much as I do the wonderful contribution made by agriculture during the last war, the way in which, notwithstanding labour troubles and the shortage of farm machinery, they rose to the emergency and produced food supplies in quantities that were the admiration of the world; keeping all these things in mind, I say that it little behooves any member of this house, even though the motion is couched in such flowery, inoffensive language, to say in effect, in the words of the motion, that the farmers of Canada are carrying on a mode of sabotage or a sit-down strike and are declining to produce foodstuffs that the world so badly needs, simply because they are not getting high enough prices.
I wish to say to the leader of the opposition that he knows-and he should know it better than anyone in Canada-that last year, one of the years he complains about, the farmers had more acreage in production than ever before; but we had a smaller crop. Why? Simply because weather conditions were unfavourable. Are the farmers of this country to be faced with the accusation that appears in this motion, the accusation that appears in the speech of the leader of the opposition, namely that of deliberately curtailing production because the price was not right, simply because nature let them down after they had done everything that they could do?
Let us have the figures. Unlike the leader of the opposition, I do not ask anyone to take my thoughts on a subject unsupported by the facts. I hold in my hand a statement issued by the bureau of statistics, agricultural branch. Let us take wheat. Last year our
Price Ceiling-Farm Products

farmers sowed 23.4 million acres to wheat. Looking over the table that I hold in my hand, I see that over a period of six years that was the largest acreage sown to wheat in any of those years. Notwithstanding that fact, the crop yield is very much lower.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: Summer-fallow did not help it.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I am not talking about summer-fallow. The crop yield last year was 129'6 million bushels less than the previous year, although in the previous year there was less acreage sown to wheat. When one compares that with the bumper year of 1942 he will find that- the crop yield last year was still greater in deficit when compared with that other year. Is the farmer to blame; is the farmer to be maligned and that nasty innuendo go out that he has deliberately decreased production because the price is not right? I say that statement is positively untrue and should be retracted.
I now come to oats. In oats we have the same story. Last year 14-4 million acres were sown to oats, whereas in the previous year only 14-3 million acres were sown, and yet the yield is down 118 million bushels. Are the farmers to blame for that? .Is the wartime prices and trade board to blame for that? Is the price structure to blame for that? Let us follow on through with barley. All through the picture- the story is the same.
There is not a word of truth in the charge made by the leader of the opposition and in the innuendo contained in the motion that the farmers of this country have put on a sit-down strike and decline to produce as much food as they could, simply because the price structure is not right. I know the leader of the opposition would dearly love to get into power and I fancy he would do quite a bit to try to get there; but I want to tell him in the friendliest spirit that he underestimates, and he almost insults, the intelligence of the farmers of this country when he adopts the tactics that he adopted in his speech when introducing this motion -on May 6 last.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer, namely farm implements. I come from a rural riding. I know I am treading on dangerous ground when I say anything about the cost of farm implements, because over half of my electors are farmers. The house well knows that if you want to get cheers at any farm gathering all you have to do is to build up a good case against either the packers or the implement companies, and you are off to a good start. However, I believe that the present is an occasion when we should frankly

speak our minds and when we should not do anything to make a difficult situation any worse.
I am told, and I honestly believe the information to be correct, that the 12^ per cent increase recently granted to the implement industry does not compensate the industry for the increase in labour and material costs which it has experienced. If that is correct- and I believe it to be correct-and when one bears in mind the fact that we so badly need the implements, is it not the part of wisdom to make it possible for our farmers to get these implements? I have been told by farmer friends that the implement situation is so bad that at auction sales secondhand machines are selling for almost as much as new implements.

Here are the figures. I am making this statement so that it will be on the record. It is estimated that if the implement companies do everything that they hope to this year they will produce in Canada just under S34 million worth of Canadian-built implements. What is 12) per cent on $34 million? It is $4-25 million. Now I ask my hon. friends in the Conservative opposition on the other side of the house, who are moaning about these increases in the prices of farm implements, to relate that $4-25 million to the total farm income, which is over $1,600 million. What do you get? You reach a figure of less than one-tenth of one per cent. There is another point to consider. The life of most of these implements is more than ten years, so you divide that figure of

Price Ceiling-Farm Products
one-tenth of one per cent by ten, and reach the figure of one one-hundredth of one per cent.
I suggest that we have reached a time in our economy when we have to be courageous enough to speak our minds, if we are to get anywhere, and when we have to face this problem in a businesslike fashion instead of trying to whip up the sectional feelings of the people.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
In rising to support the amendment moved by the leader of this party, I wish to state briefly the views of a large number of western farmers to whom I have spoken about the matters contained in the amendment, particularly one subject which is dealt with in these words:
. . . the government's price ceiling policies . . . are imposing on the food producers of Canada an unfair share of the burden of maintaining the government's price stabilization policies.
The farmers of western Canada believe that, and feel strongly about it.
However, before going on with that point, I should like to say it seems to me that most of the complaints of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver), who has just taken his seat, against this party boil down to the petulant complaint that this party has not yet published an agricultural price control policy for the government to follow. Had we done so probably we would have been fine fellows. The hon. gentleman accused the leader of this party of belittling the farmers by saying they were going on a sit-down strike, and so forth. I am not a bit afraid to say that as far as the hog producers of Alberta are concerned they have gone on at least a semi-sit-down strike. A certain number of them have definitely quit raising hogs entirely because of the prices they have received in relation to the price they could get for the barley, while large numbers of others have considerably reduced their hog production. This is at least one definite instance where you have a refusal on the part of farmers to produce an extremely important commodity because of the price policy of the government.

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext: It would not be because of a shortage of coarse feeds?

maintopic: PRICE CEILING POLICIES 'WITH RESPECT TO FARM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
If you will look up the figures of the shipments of coarse grains from Alberta to eastern Canada you will find that it was not due to any shortage of coarse grains.	.
Before going farther, I should like also to say to hon. gentlemen to my immediate left, who are extremely fond of poking gibes at the members of this party and of accusing
them of inconsistency, and so on, that they would do much better to devote themselves to educating, public opinion, if that is the proper word, to their ideas rather than spending so much time in this house attacking ours.
In that connection, I should like to make it plain that there is one fundamental conception as far as I am concerned on which my remarks are based. It is that artificial control of prices and arbitrary distribution of commodities are contrary to the conceptions of free trade and free enterprise under which Canada has developed from the very beginning and in which the great majority of the people of this country quite evidently believe, as shown by the results of the last federal election. Artificial controls are the essence of a socialistic state, and the people of this dominion demonstrated at the polls that they do not want a socialistic state, as evidenced by their lack of support for hon. members to my left. So that I think we may take it for granted as something definite that everyone will admit that the majority of the people of this country are believers in free enterprise. In view of that fact, I think all believers in free enterprise, including the government, who profess so to believe, should now be bending their thoughts and energies toward the abolition of all those controls which were forced upon us during the war. One evil at least, of price control has been well demonstrated in this and many other debates we have had in this house. That is, you have endless arguments as to how these price controls should be worked, which should be upped, which should be taken off, which should be reduced, and so forth, all of which is motivated essentially by the desire on the part of each economic group in the country to improve its lot at the expense of some other group.
To come back to the western farmer for whom I intend to speak chiefly, even among those who are socialistically inclined the realization has finally spread that they are bearing almost the entire burden of price controls on many agricultural products, particularly on wheat. As a result, there is now a very widespread feeling in the west that we should get world market prices for our grain. Along with this is the almost universal belief that if the government will not permit the people of the west to obtain world prices; if it is to continue price controls on farm products and thus subsidize the consumer in Europe as well as the consumer in Canada, then all the taxpayers in Canada should shoulder the load equally instead of leaving it to the farmer to pay the shot.

speechtext:
The proposition gets down to this. The meat producer is being called upon to subsidize the general consuming public just the same as the wheat producer is being called upon to subsidize that public as well as overseas markets. I think that is a just statement to make. The proposition that the government price control policy has placed a heavy burden on the western farmer has been adequately proved, not just by what I have had to say but by what other hon. members have said in this house from time to time. I do not think there is any doubt that the government price control policy will have the result of reducing production.
There is no use in blinking our eyes at that or trying to throw up a smoke-screen. It is being said it is disgraceful that the farmers should be carrying on a sit-down strike, but I 
think we may as well admit that if the farmer or anyone else cannot get a fair return for his labour he will not try to put his product on the market if he can avoid doing so. In view of the unfairness to the western farmer, I feel I must call upon the government to raise the , ceilings on agricultural products if they will j not abolish them altogether. If it is desired that our own people shall be able to buy bread cheaply; if it is desired that the people in the j overseas countries shall be able to do the same thing, then the cost of the necessary subsidies should be borne by the country as a whole and not be placed upon the shoulders of the western farmer.
